title: Trust at Scale: Nam Nguyen on How TruthSystems is Building the Framework for Safe AI in Law
author: Nam Nguyen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: Moore accepts the need to move beyond product information and materially develops the cluster’s procurement proposition with a structured, client-specific selection process involving needs assessment, stakeholder input, demonstrations, shortlisting and recommendations. However, the account is promotional and provides no independent evidence that the process improves adoption, renewal value or realised outcomes.
qs: We actually offer a technology selection service, which is a six-step advisory framework we’ve designed to help our clients choose the right solution for them.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI needs a specialist layer around general model capability and materially extends the cluster by framing trust-and-safety infrastructure—especially supervisory agents and embedded legal and ethical guardrails—as a practical requirement for adoption. It supports this as a research-led product thesis, not with demonstrated operational effectiveness.
qs: And there we started tackling, as you said, the number one problem for law,  adopting AI, was trust, and our first pass at it was, okay, can we embed legal and ethical guardrails into…  every AI interactions for lawyers.
We’re trying to build the infrastructure for trust and safety that makes it real and actionable for law firms today.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Nguyen accepts the cluster’s core claims that legal AI is jagged, requires verification and must be governed within redesigned workflows. He materially extends them with a concrete platform-agnostic governance layer that applies adaptive controls across tools, enforces task-specific use rules and monitors risks in real time.
qs: I think when we talk about these two paradigms, it’s about regulating AI not from the outside, but to make AI part of that solutions, where governance can lives and breathe within the workflow, and we can transform trust and safety from something people say or just a checkbox that we’re trying to get through to a dynamic system that learns and adapts.

And one of the things we like to work with firms, or we’re already working with firms with is how can we enforce behavioral guardrails, making sure that you’re using the right tools for the right use cases.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: Nguyen accepts that trust depends on governance beyond error-free output and materially extends the workflow framing upstream: firms must control inputs, restrict unapproved tools and respect client authorisation. His intercepted memo example also shows human review preventing an inaccurate output from reaching the client, while identifying unauthorised tool use as a separate breach of trust.
qs: Nam Nguyen (11:36)  Yeah, I mean, we do believe that just in regulated fields like law, the biggest risks actually begin with the input, right?

But  Marlene Gebauer (12:36)  you  Nam Nguyen (12:40)  There’s also a fundamental level of violations here where you’re going against the rules of engagement you have with your clients for using those unapproved tools.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Nguyen directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that effective continuous learning requires selective filtering rather than chasing every AI release. He recommends returning to fundamentals and using grounded, practical governance guidance; his broader firm-controlled governance proposals are compatible with the cluster’s emphasis on strategically guided experimentation.
qs: I just kind of believe that if you chase every new trends and new publications going out there, you essentially will chase the marketing cycle.
And I think, you  true understanding comes here from revisiting a lot of fundamentals.

kp.k: AI can govern AI within lawyers’ workflows
kp.d: Nguyen argues that AI should be both subject to governance and infrastructure for implementing it. He proposes supervisory systems that interpret policies and unstructured data to alert lawyers to confidentiality, compliance and ethical risks in real time, contrasting this oversight function with copilots assisting research and review. This is a design argument and product vision, not a demonstrated safety finding.
qs: First, AI as a subject, think a lot of people agree it’s a very powerful technology that needs oversight, accountability, and guardrails.
how can we build a AI risk supervisors where we’re building an extra pair of eyes alerting lawyers
of risk in real time, such as violating potential confidentiality, compliance, or even ethical violations.

kp.k: Input governance addresses risks beyond fabricated outputs
kp.d: Nguyen asserts that major risks in regulated legal work begin with inputs and tool access, not simply generated answers. He recounts an unnamed firm's associate drafting a hallucination-riddled memo in unapproved ChatGPT despite a client's prior-approval requirement; the firm caught it before further use. The anecdote illustrates a separate client-trust and authorization breach, rather than establishing an incidence rate or a court sanctions incident.
qs: we do believe that just in regulated fields like law, the biggest risks actually begin with the input
their client has told the law firms to only use AI after they
approved it. Now, one of the associates at the time actually drafted a memo in ChatGPT, unapproved tools, and it was riddled with hallucinations.
There’s also a fundamental level of violations here where you’re going against the rules of engagement you have with your clients for using those unapproved tools.

kp.k: Charter translates restrictions into real-time controls
kp.d: Nguyen describes Charter as a platform deploying access controls and guardrails across vendor applications and internally built programs, appearing as a browser extension for lawyers, paralegals and staff. Its stated function is to operationalize firm policies and client restrictions before potential breaches. The transcript supplies product descriptions but no measured effectiveness or coverage results.
qs: Charter basically at the core is a platform that allows firms to deploy access controls and guardrails to all of their, you know, ⁓ vendor AI applications or even like programs that they’re building themselves.
we are a browser extensions that basically can help firms monitor and alert before they can potentially violate any firms restrictions.
or client restrictions in real time.

kp.k: Approved tools still require use-case restrictions
kp.d: Nguyen argues that approval of an AI application does not make it suitable for every task. He specifically characterizes Copilot as unsuitable for legal research and advocates behavioral guardrails enforcing firms’ intended uses. Gebauer separately suggests that innovation, knowledge-management and research teams can supply tool-selection expertise and notes the difficulty practitioners face reconciling multiple policies and client guidelines.
qs: what you are having in your hands is a host of tools that can do basically everything, but can it do everything well? Probably not, right?
copilot is very powerful in every single interactions, but it’s not suitable for you to do legal research on them.
how can we enforce behavioral guardrails, making sure that you’re using the right tools for the right use cases.
maybe where your innovation or your KM or your research people are coming in and giving information about like, yeah, these tools are good for this and these other tools are good for something else.

kp.k: Governance should operate continuously rather than remain static
kp.d: Nguyen recommends embedding policy guidance in individual AI interactions rather than relying on periodically drafted documents that users forget. He describes different needs across adoption stages: initial access controls and alignment with client guidelines for newer adopters, versus demonstrating controls to clients for more mature adopters. These observations come from his reported interactions with firms, without a stated sample.
qs: we’ve seen such a spectrum of response because we see really a spectrum of where firms are in their AI adoption journey
how can we operationalize governance, not just something where firms come together once every quarter
then it becomes something that just rots or being forgotten in a SharePoint somewhere.
We want like policies and governance to lives at every single interactions to guide the users in the right directions.

kp.k: Retrieval augmentation does not eliminate hallucinations
kp.d: Nguyen argues that retrieval-augmented generation can fail at both retrieval and generation: legal context, jurisdictions and definitions complicate evidence selection, while confident generation may proceed from wrong evidence. Reporting his interpretation of OpenAI's Why Language Models Hallucinate paper, he attributes unsupported answering to incentives penalizing uncertainty and benchmark competition. He proposes smaller, more predictable models rewarded for detecting contradictions; no comparative performance measurements are presented.
qs: the problem exists at both the R, the retrieval part and the G, the generation stage
the model generates it very confidently, but it’s based on kind of the wrong evidence.
OpenAI actually recently produced a paper called Why Language Models Hallucinate.
So they actually lose points in training for saying, don’t know.
We want to make smaller but more predictable models that are rewarded for spotting contradictions.

kp.d: Asked about improvements in legal RAG systems, Nguyen reports seeing incremental vendor progress but declines to predict that more compute and better evaluations will necessarily solve reliability problems. He describes competing views on scaling and reports Richard Sutton's skepticism about the LLM paradigm. His expectation of eventually adequate performance is explicitly hopeful, not an established result or dated forecast.
qs: people are very divided on, you know, how scaling laws would play out.
At end of the day, the answer is we will kind of have to wait and see.

I do see that every vendor is getting a little bit better at it and hopefully with the scale and the interest and the money that is going into this field that we will get into an endpoint where it is good enough, I believe.

kp.k: Independent governance addresses fragmented AI ecosystems
kp.d: Nguyen argues that firms will continue using multiple platforms and building custom workflows even after buying products such as Harvey or CoCounsel. He positions a platform-agnostic governance layer as complementary to those vendors, allowing firms to maintain their own policies, client restrictions and confidentiality requirements across tools without depending on individual vendors’ development schedules. This is his strategic rationale, not evidence that universal coverage has been achieved.
qs: governance is only as good as its coverage.
even when firms are buying a Harvey and a co-counsel, they won’t live inside a single platform.
firms can kind of define, enforce, and evolve with their own policies that they don’t have to wait for another vendor’s roadmap.
The firm’s ethical standards, their client restrictions, the confidentiality rules move with them.

kp.k: Funding targets measurable, client-facing AI assurance
kp.d: Lambert reports a $4 million seed round led by Gradient Ventures and Lightspeed. In response, Nguyen says investment will support visibility into AI use across vendors, clients and matters, with innovation and risk teams co-developing and testing capabilities in live settings. The intended shift is from publicizing tool purchases to demonstrating responsible use and client value; these are investment plans, not reported outcome improvements.
qs: you’ve just announced a major $4 million seed round led by Gradient Ventures and Lightspeed.
move from adopting AI to governing it in a measurable and client facing way.
real time visibility into how AI is being used across, you know, all your vendors, your clients and matters.
partner with innovations and risk teams inside of these firms to co-develop and test these capabilities in live environments

kp.k: Governance data could become a competitive differentiator
kp.d: Nguyen predicts that visibility into who uses AI, on which platforms and with what outcomes will distinguish firms. He reports a current project measuring usage across vendors for client-facing reporting and hopes to compare results against baselines. Responding to Lambert's engagement-letter question, he also identifies business-development materials as a possible use. Claims that governance will strengthen trust and help firms win remain prospective; no baseline comparisons or client outcomes are supplied.
qs: I think engagement letter is one thing, but even just business development materials too.
hopefully we have the ability to work with Firm on benchmarking it against like, what is the baseline?
one of the most exciting projects we’re doing right now is actually helping firms measure AI usage across all their vendors
governance and compliance will no longer be blockers.
we want it to become the differentiators

kp.k: Shared AI access pressures firms to differentiate strategically
kp.d: Discussing a commentator he admires, Nguyen endorses the view that firms must innovate their business models rather than merely adopt AI. He argues that corporate in-house counsel already have access to the same tools, so provider advantage depends on strategic application and moving upmarket. This is a competitive-market argument, not evidence of quantified insourcing or changes in fees or staffing.
qs: essentially what we are in this race for is the race with also our own clients because the in-house councils, they already have access to the same tools.
AI strategically to move up market as well.
we should innovate the business model and not just sheerly adopt the technology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nguyen argues that AI can provide governance infrastructure within legal workflows, rather than merely being a technology subject to external oversight.
pts.d: At 07:53–09:37, Nguyen proposes AI risk supervisors that interpret policies and unstructured data to alert lawyers to confidentiality, compliance and ethical risks in real time. He contrasts an AI copilot helping perform legal tasks with an additional monitoring layer. At 10:33 and 16:40–17:45, he describes Charter as a browser-extension platform for access controls and behavioral guardrails, intended to turn static firm policies and client restrictions into operational guidance. These are descriptions of product capabilities and ambitions, not demonstrated findings about reductions in violations.

pts.k: Nguyen claims that important legal-AI risks arise at the input stage, including unauthorized tool use and using approved tools for unsuitable tasks.
pts.d: At 11:36–15:39, Nguyen argues that checking generated answers alone cannot address breaches of client permissions or confidentiality. His example concerns an associate using unapproved ChatGPT to draft a memo despite a client's prior-approval requirement. The firm caught the hallucination-riddled memo; the potential public consequences and lasting damage to client trust are hypothetical. He also argues that tool approval should be use-case-specific, asserting that Microsoft Copilot is not suitable for legal research. Charter's proposed response is to govern both access and behavior before a violation occurs.

pts.k: Nguyen says retrieval-augmented generation does not eliminate hallucinations, and remains uncertain whether continued model scaling will deliver sufficiently reliable legal AI.
pts.d: At 18:27–22:53, Nguyen identifies two failure points: retrieval can select legally inappropriate context, including jurisdictional or definitional mismatches, and generation can confidently answer on that wrong basis. He invokes an OpenAI paper to explain incentives to answer rather than express uncertainty, then contrasts that approach with TruthSystems' aim to build smaller, more predictable models rewarded for detecting contradictions. He reports incremental vendor improvement but does not claim reliability has been solved. His discussion of automated contradiction detection is not evidence that human verification can be dispensed with.

pts.k: Nguyen predicts that firms will continue operating multi-tool AI environments, making platform-independent governance valuable.
pts.d: At 27:29–29:11, Nguyen argues that integrated legal-AI products do not cover the whole firm's activity. His stated bet is that firms will keep adopting tools and developing internal workflows, including through technology acquisitions. An independent governance layer would allow firms to apply and update their own policies across Harvey, CoCounsel and internal applications without depending on any single vendor's roadmap. This is a strategic market prediction and intended product benefit, not a quantified adoption forecast.

pts.k: Nguyen predicts a shift from announcing AI adoption to demonstrating responsible use and client outcomes, with governance becoming a competitive differentiator.
pts.d: At 23:56–26:42 and 32:00–33:58, Nguyen argues that visibility into AI usage across vendors, clients and matters will enable firms to demonstrate compliance and value. He anticipates using this information in engagement letters and business-development materials, potentially with comparisons against a baseline. His structural forecast is that usage, adoption and outcome data will distinguish firms, turning governance from a perceived obstacle into a means of scaling innovation. He describes measuring cross-vendor usage as a current project, while client-outcome improvement and market success remain hoped-for benefits.

pts.k: Nguyen argues that clients' access to the same AI tools pushes law firms to differentiate through strategic application rather than access alone.
pts.d: At 29:45–31:34, while discussing resources he admires, Nguyen expresses his own view that firms are in a competitive race involving their in-house clients. He says the edge comes from applying AI strategically to move upmarket. This is a qualitative competitive claim, not evidence of actual changes in insourcing, revenue, staffing or market share.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Nguyen's research and firm-facing experience, one anonymous incident, technical reasoning and cited authority; no quantitative effectiveness results are supplied.
pts.d: Nguyen grounds the urgency of governance in reactions to presentations of Stanford supervisory-agent work to policymakers and law-firm risk functions (02:58–05:38), and in interactions with firms at different adoption stages (06:33–07:40). The unapproved ChatGPT memo is an anonymous firsthand case from that research setting, not a named court-sanctions incident or a measured hallucination rate. His RAG account draws on his own writing and the OpenAI paper 'Why Language Models Hallucinate'; his uncertainty about scaling also references Richard Sutton. No benchmark results, sample sizes, measured reduction in risk, client-value comparisons or competitive-outcome data are reported. The announced $4 million funding supports product-development plans, not proof of effectiveness.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Nguyen distinguishes current governance needs and product work from an undated, conditional vision of competitive transformation.
pts.d: In this 2025 interview, Nguyen presents policy enforcement and access controls as present needs and Charter as an existing platform. Cross-vendor measurement and development with innovation and risk teams are described as ongoing work, with seed funding intended to expand visibility and client assurance. The broader forecast has no calendar deadline. Its conditions include coverage across the firm's AI ecosystem, task-appropriate tool use, alignment with firm and client restrictions, and an ability to show responsible use and outcomes. Better RAG reliability is explicitly uncertain and linked to continued improvement, investment and evaluation. Competitive success is framed as a hope for firms investing in these capabilities, not a guaranteed result.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms, their lawyers and staff, internal governance teams, corporate clients and AI vendors.
pts.d: For firms early in adoption, Nguyen describes help establishing access controls and aligning use with outside counsel guidelines; for mature adopters, he emphasizes client-facing assurance and differentiation. Lawyers, associates, paralegals and staff would experience real-time guidance and restrictions in their workflows. Innovation and risk teams would co-develop controls and gain usage visibility. Clients would receive evidence of compliance with their restrictions and, prospectively, evidence of value and outcomes. In-house counsel appear as buyers with access to the same AI tools, creating pressure on firms to differentiate strategically. Vendors would operate within firm-controlled, cross-platform governance rather than supply the only governance boundary. TruthSystems is presented as a governance software provider, not an alternative legal service provider. No concrete prediction about lawyer displacement, staffing ratios, fees or access to justice is made.
